segments.text: Ultrasenography of the Inferia Vena Cava
In this video, we'll show you how to perform an ultrasound scan of the Inferia Vena Cava,
which we'll refer to as the IVC from now on.
The most common reason to perform a point-of-care scan of the IVC
is to assess volume status.
We'll talk about that a little later,
but first, we'll go over the basics of how to perform a scan.
The abdominal IVC is retroperitoneal and closely adjacent to the aorta.
To assess the IVC, we first scan in the short axis or transverse plane and center the vessel
on the screen.
We then rotate to the long axis or sagittal plane for a longitudinal view of the IVC.
We can use a curvilinear or phased array probe for the scans, short axis view.
Place the probe just under the zyfoid process with the probe indicator pointing to the patient's
right side.
Pushing the probe down firmly can improve the image by displacing any overlying abdominal
gas.
You can now clearly make out two anico-extructures, lying just anterior to the hyper-echoic
vertebral body and its large acoustic shadow.
To the left of the image, just to the right of the patient's midline, is the IVC.
To the right of the image, just to the left of the patient's midline, you can see the abdominal aorta.
The IVC has a thinner wall than the aorta, and can usually be compressed quite easily with the probe.
In contrast, the aorta is thick walled and almost impossible to compress, remaining circular under the probe.
It also pulsates much more noticeably than the IVC.
Long Axis View
The easiest way to obtain a long axis view of the IVC is to obtain the short axis view first and then transition.
To do this, center the vessel and then rotate the probe 90 degrees until the probe indicator faces the patient's head.
Alternatively, you can go directly to the long axis view.
Place the probe just under the zyfoid process with the indicator facing the patient's head.
Now, slide or fan the probe very slightly to the patient's right until the IVC is visible.
Here, you can see the IVC in longitudinal section at the lower edge of the image.
The arrows illustrate the direction of blood flow from coddle to cranial.
You can sometimes see subtle cardiac cycle-related pulsation of the IVC.
You should also be able to see respiratory variation in the IVC's diameter, which normally
partially collapses in inspiration. To measure the IVC diameter, freeze the image, then take
measurements at peak expiration and inspiration. Use the caliper or measurement button to draw
a line at a right angle to the vessel's long axis. You can measure either just distal to
where the IVC enters the right atrium, or two centimeters proximal to the junction of
the IVC and hepatic vein. A large diameter and reduced respiratory variation may suggest
volume overload or increased right heart pressures. A small diameter and increased
variation, on the other hand, may suggest volume depletion. Okay, now that you have
an overview of IVC ultrasound skills, check out the Pocus article on Ambus.
